Representatives of the Hungarian wedding industry raised around 3 million forints for the Bethesda children's hospital at the 13th Hungarian Wedding Gala.

Representatives of Hungary's wedding industry raised around 3 million Hungarian Forints (€8.218,18) for a children's hospital at the 13th Hungarian Wedding Gala.

The evening saw awards presented across 19 different categories, recognising achievements within the wedding industry.

Charity is an important tradition at the annual gala. This year, proceeds from ticket sales and raffle coupons went towards purchasing surgical drills for bone surgery for the Bethesda Children's Hospital.

Founder and chief organiser Katalin Landesz revealed that the cooperation with Bethesda "began with a tragic event".

“The son of our colleague suffered burns in a high-voltage electrical accident. The news deeply affected the entire industry, and that year we decided that the Wedding Gala would support her and her family to help her recover," Landesz told Euronews.

"This is now the third year we have supported the hospital. We either purchase another piece of life-saving equipment or take on a renovation project".

Earlier this year, more than 40 wedding industry professionals transformed the surgical departments at the Bethesda Children's Hospital in just two days.

The renovation brought a fresh look to the space, with decorations inspired by the four seasons and nearby city park. Every detail was thoughtfully designed to create a more child-friendly environment for young patients.

The volunteers also gifted furniture and custom designed curtains to the hospital and also renovated the washroom facilities.

A wildlife rehabilitation centre received an unusual report of venomous vipers sheltering in a water meter chamber, these however, turned out to be harmless slow worms.

Just under two dozen slow worms, initially mistaken for venomous vipers, were found in a water meter chamber in southern Poland.

Wildlife rehabilitation centre Leśne Pogotowie received a report that venomous vipers had taken refuge in the underground chamber. However, rescuers found 19 slow worms sheltering from the cold weather instead.

The chamber provided ideal conditions, with its cool, damp environment protecting the worms' winter torpor, and the concrete structure offering protetion from freezing temperatures.

The smooth, vertical walls of the chamber meant the slow worms easily descended down into the space, but had no way of climbing back to the surface.

After being rescued from the chamber, the slow worms could be not be released straight back into nature. Instead, they were taken to the animal rehabilitation shelter.

At this time of year, the reptiles were already in a state of winter torpor. Releasing them in cold conditions would leave them with little time to find a new shelter.

At the centre, the slow worms will be provided with the right conditions to spend the winter. A stable, low temperature allows them to remain in hibernation and reduces the risk of unnecessary waking.

The slow worms will only be returned to the wild in spring, when temperature are high enough.

What is a slow worm?

With their serpentine appearance, slow worms are often mistaken for snakes. In reality, they are actually legless lizards.

They are non-venomous and do not pose a threat to humans. In fact, the creatures are beneficial garden residents, as they feed on snails, earthworms and other small invertebrates.

Poland is home to two species of slow worms, the common slow worm and the eastern slow worm. The two species are very similar, but differ, among other things, in the structure and arrangement of their scales. Many males of the eastern slow worm have characteristic blue spots on their backs.

They can be mainly found in the south eastern region of Poland.

The crowd protested on Sunday afternoon against government plans affecting Czech public television and radio. It was the largest rally so far against the three-party government led by Prime Minister Andrej Babis.

Hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Prague on Sunday to defend the independence of public television and radio and oppose the government's plans to change their funding system. The demonstration was organised by the civic organisation Million Moments for Democracy. Its slogan, "Never again 4:36", refers to the time when the government majority pushed through a controversial amendment to the law in the Chamber of Deputies at first reading in mid-October. The vote took place in the early hours of Saturday morning, after the majority cut short the plenary debate, denying more than 60 opposition MPs the opportunity to speak.

At Letná, Prague's largest square, an estimated 350,000 to 400,000 people took part in the protest against the government's plans and policies, according to media reports on Sunday afternoon.

Protesters who had come from many parts of the country sharply criticised the government's policies and demanded that the coalition party Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD), led by Tomio Okamura, the speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, withdraw from the government.

While the two public service broadcasters are currently funded by the population through compulsory monthly subscription fees, the government wants to finance them from the state budget in future. The proposal has provoked significant public resistance, as many fear that the government could exert influence over the editorial independence and impartiality of the two broadcasters.

According to publicly available data, this future state subsidy would be much lower than the current licence-fee revenues of public television and radio.

The opposition, the press and a significant part of public opinion also oppose the changes because they fear that state funding of public service media would restrict their freedom.

At the demonstration, student organisations at universities and colleges in the Czech Republic, dozens of Czech theatres, writers, numerous top athletes, churches, healthcare workers and representatives of international journalists' organisations also expressed their support for public television and radio.

Speakers repeatedly stressed at the protest that public service media cannot be the property of politicians, the government or the state, but belong to everyone and must reflect the views of all significant sections of society. They also called for independent and free public media.

In the Czech Republic, every household that owns a television or radio is required to pay a monthly fee of 150 koruna (2,400 forint) for television and 55 koruna (880 forint) for radio. This year, Czech Television's revenue from these fees amounts to 6.73 billion koruna (107.68 billion forint), while Czech Radio receives 2.47 billion koruna (39.52 billion forint).

The Babiš government has announced that it would abolish the household fees and instead fund the two public service broadcasters through the state budget. The Prague demonstration was broadcast live by the public news television channel, the CTK news agency and a few independent media outlets. Radek Vondráček of the strongest governing party, Elégedetlen Polgárok Akciója (ANO), condemned the organisers of the protest and the organisation Million Moments for Democracy in a television debate programme, calling them "an association of professional agitators".

According to police reports, the demonstration proceeded without incident until early evening, and there were no disturbances.

For veteran Santas, the challenge is not simply knowing the latest toys, but making every child feel heard and preserving the magic of Christmas.

The Philippines is building closer military ties with Australia, Japan and the US as tensions with China continue in the South China Sea. The partnerships cover joint exercises, surveillance equipment and closer coordination between their forces.

Australia and the Philippines signed a defence agreement on Sunday to make joint patrols, military exercises and disaster relief operations easier to organise, Philippine officials said.

Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr and Australian Ambassador Marc Innes-Brown signed the agreement in Manila, with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese attending the ceremony during his visit for regional summits.

The Defence Cooperation Arrangement updates a 1995 agreement. It builds on a separate visiting forces agreement, in force since 2012, which already allows troops from each country to train on the other’s territory.

Teodoro said the new arrangement would simplify the procedures for carrying out joint activities.

“Rather than 100 steps to do a single thing, it will just now take 10,” he told reporters, according to Reuters.

He said closer cooperation between the countries’ naval, air and ground forces would help the Philippines deter threats, including in the South China Sea.

Australia said the agreement covered information sharing, military planning and training, monitoring activity at sea and developing defence infrastructure.

Asked whether the pact was intended to counter China, Albanese said: “This isn’t aimed at any one country. This is about supporting sovereignty of every country.”

He said most Australian trade passed through the South China Sea and stressed the importance of keeping shipping routes open.

Australia also announced additional funding for its Southeast Asia Maritime Partnerships programme. It will provide regional partners with aerial and surface drones, secure communications equipment and training to help detect and respond to threats at sea and cyberattacks. The announcement did not give a funding figure.

Manila expands its defence partnerships

The agreement follows several recent steps by the Philippines to strengthen military ties with its partners.

On 9 November, Japan agreed to supply coastal radar and surveillance drones to the Philippine military under a 4.3 billion yen (€24 million) grant. The equipment is intended to help monitor ships in waters around the country.

In a statement released on 10 November, Australia, Japan, the Philippines and the United States also committed to a joint military coordination centre in the Philippines. They agreed to coordinate defence investments and expand joint exercises.

China’s claims in the South China Sea overlap with those of the Philippines and several other Southeast Asian countries. Beijing has previously criticised Manila’s joint military activities with its partners, saying they increase regional tensions.

An international tribunal ruled in 2016 that China’s claims of historic rights to resources had no legal basis where they exceeded the rights granted by the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Beijing rejects the ruling.

The object, known as "1998 KY26", about 11 metres wide, is moving near Earth; yet something other than the Sun's or Earth's gravity seems to affect its path and speed.

A mysterious object speeding through the Solar System has shown unusual acceleration, raising speculation that it could be a spacecraft from the former Soviet Union that went missing nearly 40 years ago.

Known as 1998 KY26, the object is an 11-metre-wide body passing near Earth. Scientists have noticed that its trajectory cannot be fully explained by the gravitational pull of the Sun or Earth.

This unusual behaviour is known as "non-gravitational acceleration", meaning that forces other than gravity are influencing the object's path and speed.

NASA chief Jared Isaacman said on Thursday that the agency is monitoring KY26 but stressed there is no reason for concern. He reassured the public that the object poses no known threat to Earth and that there is no evidence it could collide with our planet.

Has Phobos 1 been found?

A group of researchers has put forward an unusual explanation. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and two colleagues, Adam Hibberd and Adam Crowl, believe KY26 could be Phobos 1, an unmanned Soviet spacecraft launched on 7 July 1988. The probe lost contact with Earth while on its way to Mars.

The researchers built a simplified model of Phobos 1 and compared how it would reflect sunlight as it rotated with observations of KY26. They found that the model closely matched eight separate sets of observations of the object.

KY26 reflects almost 52% of the sunlight that hits it and completes one full rotation every 5.35 minutes. Loeb and his colleagues argue that these characteristics are consistent with their hypothesis that KY26 could be an artificial object.

New study challenges the dark comet theory

One explanation, first proposed in a 2023 study, is that KY26 is a so-called 'dark comet' containing trapped water that turns into gas, creating thrust as the object moves through space. However, astronomers have not detected the cloud of gas or tail normally associated with comets.

A separate scientific study has offered a contrasting explanation. Researchers concluded that 1998 KY26 is most likely a dehydrated asteroid. This would mean that water ice is unlikely to be responsible for its unusual acceleration, as temperatures are too high for sufficient ice to survive over an extended period.

Another possible explanation is solar radiation, which can exert pressure on the object's surface and slightly alter its trajectory.

Other observations also point towards a natural, rocky asteroid rather than an old spacecraft. A study published in the journal Nature Communications in 2025 estimated its diameter at just 11 metres.

Japanese spacecraft could solve the mystery

A Japanese space mission could eventually provide important answers. The Hayabusa2 spacecraft is due to reach 1998 KY26 in July 2031 and study it at close range. It would be the first mission to directly investigate an asteroid of this tiny size.

Images and measurements taken during the encounter could reveal whether the object is indeed a natural rocky body or potentially something artificial.

Until then, Avi Loeb's suggestion remains a fascinating but unproven theory. The Harvard astrophysicist has even joked that Hayabusa2's cameras might discover a label reading "Made in the U.S.S.R." rather than a block of ice.

Directed by Hélène Lam Trong, "Dans Gaza" won the best documentary prize at Montreal's Cinemania festival. This 72-minute film immerses in the daily lives of four AFP Palestinian journalists, who covered the first months of the war at the risk of their lives.

This award shines a light on the work of those who have continued to inform the world from Gaza.

The documentary "Dans Gaza", directed by Hélène Lam Trong (source in French), was awarded on Saturday 14 November the prize for best documentary film at the Cinemania Francophone Film Festival in Montreal. Over 72 minutes, the film follows four Agence France-Presse journalists: Mai Yaghi, reporter, Adel Zaanoun, Gaza bureau coordinator, and photojournalists Mahmud Hams and Mohammed Abed.

The documentary portrays the first seven months after the Hamas attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023. With free access to the enclave blocked, international media then relied on Palestinian journalists on the ground to document the conflict.

For more than 200 days, these four reporters worked under bombardment, despite the danger, while facing the same shortages as the rest of the population. At the same time, they had to protect their families, who were directly exposed to the war.

A film made without ever being able to enter Gaza

A journalist for around twenty years, Hélène Lam Trong gradually shifted towards documentary filmmaking. She notably directed "Daech, les enfants fantômes", which earned her the Albert Londres audiovisual prize in 2023.

For "Dans Gaza", she was approached by AFP in January 2024, three months after the start of the war.

Yet the director was never able to travel to the Palestinian enclave. Free access for the international press was banned there by the Israeli army.

The four reporters had agreed to testify, but no one knew whether they would ever manage to leave Gaza. When they were eventually evacuated with their families through Egypt, the director met them in Cairo. The film was built from their accounts and above all from the footage they themselves had shot as part of their work for AFP. Nearly 85% of the documentary is based on their own images.

In Montreal, it was Adel Zaanoun who accepted the prize (source in French) on behalf of the team. He dedicated it to the journalists killed in the war in Gaza, but also to those who continue to work in the field, "without food, without water, without internet, without anything".

Heading for the Oscars?

Made in 2025, "Dans Gaza" is a Franco-Belgian co-production bringing together Factstory Docs, AFP's documentary subsidiary, ARTE France and RTBF.

The film had already been recognised at Sunny Side of the Doc in La Rochelle, before winning in April 2026 both the Grand Prix and the Audience Award at FIGRA, then two prizes in July at the Doc Edge festival in New Zealand, for best international documentary and best editing.

A trajectory that now opens the way for a possible nomination at the 2027 Oscars in the best documentary category.

A key event combining luxury and charity, the Hospices de Beaune wine auction is this year constrained by the meagre harvest after the summer heatwaves.

After six months of near-drought, the harvest has been cut by around half on the 60 hectares of the Hospices de Beaune, owners of a highly prestigious wine estate. Across Burgundy as a whole, it is 26% less than the average of the past five years.

Only 432 barrels and two feuillettes (half-barrels) are being offered this year in Beaune. That is close to the 358.5 barrels in 2021, the lowest level in the modern history of the auctions launched in 1859, the second oldest charitable wine sale in the world.

The recent halt to surging prices should therefore be confirmed among the roughly 500 buyers who began raising their paddles shortly before 3 p.m. under the Beaune market hall, the "capital" of Burgundy wines.

The record of 29 million euros in total takings set in 2022, with 817 barrels, therefore looks unlikely to be beaten.

"Attention, climate sceptics: climate disruption is here", says Ludivine Griveau, vineyard manager at the Hospices. "It has already been going on for some time but now we can see it in all its intensity".

Live from New York

Meagre harvest or not, there is nevertheless "always demand for Burgundy wines", explains Jérôme Flous, technical director of Maison Faiveley.

The local saying is likely to be borne out: "In Burgundy, people look for wine to sell. In Bordeaux, they look for ways to sell it".

"There will always be money for Burgundy", confirms Domaine de Montille's cellar master, American Brian Sieve. Although limited in quantity, the 2026 vintage is "incredible" in terms of quality, he says between tastings in the Hospices vat room where buyers are sampling Pommard and other Meursaults that will go under the hammer.

The heavy rains in the winter of 2025/2026 saved the vines during the extremely hot and dry summer of 2026.

Registrations from buyers are already "numerous and coming from a large number of countries", says Marie-Anne Ginoux, managing director of Sotheby's France, which is running the sale.

In the United States, despite Trump's customs duties, demand is such that an immersive room allowing people to follow the sale remotely has been set up at the New York headquarters of the auction house.

Market "globally tight"

While the record for total takings looks hard to beat, the record for the average price per barrel should "probably" fall, predicts Anne-Laure Rayne-Helfrich, marketing director of Maison François Martenot, the second largest buyer by volume at the Beaune auctions.

"French customers and clients around the world want to buy", she says, while acknowledging that the market is "globally tight". In China in particular, "the luxury sector is collapsing", explains one broker, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The Beaune sale, although it is a global showcase for luxury, is above all a charity event, since the proceeds fund structural investments for the hospital run by the Hospices, for which they receive no subsidies.

In addition to this main cause, the "charity barrel" "barrel" here meaning a 228-litre cask, is traditionally reserved for another charitable organisation. This year it will go to two associations fighting rare diseases, including Charcot disease.

The record sale was set in 2022 at 810,000 euros, more than 2,800 euros per bottle.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten has struggled to rein in political infighting within his minority coalition, a crisis that culminated when disagreements arose over a so-called "millionaire's tax" proposed by left-wing opposition parties.

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten extended crisis talks with his coalition partners over the weekend to stave off a government collapse, after an hours-long meeting on Friday failed to reach a consensus.

The crisis stems from disagreements between Jetten's centrist D66, centre-right CDA and right-wing VVD over the country's budget plans.

The already fragile unity in Jetten's Cabinet took a hit this week when lawmakers from his centrist D66 party and the center-right Christian Democrats (CDA) agreed to amendments proposed by two center-left opposition parties — PRO and Volt — to push a tax package through the Dutch parliament in a tight vote Thursday night after a daylong debate.

But the terms of the deal — PRO's leader Jesse Klaver repeatedly called part of the agreement a “millionaire's tax” — enraged the VVD.

The proposal aims to apply a higher tax of 38.5% on returns above €60,000, for example from interest earned on savings or investments. Anyone who makes less than €60,000 in profit from assets would not have to pay this higher rate.

The crisis erupted when the plan was passed by parliament after it had clinched support from left-wing parties to push through the tax deal. The VVD, however, voted against the government's own tax plan, with party leader Dilan Yeşilgöz-Zegerius saying she had been blindsided.

VVD calls minority coalition a 'failed experiment'

Following more than seven hours of crisis talks on Friday with his coalition partners, during which the government's future hung by a thread, Jetten emerged to reveal they would stay together, for now.

But Yeşilgöz told reporters after the talks she believed "the minority cabinet is a failed experiment and it cannot go on like this".

She called for a "fundamental reset" of the coalition and even Jetten acknowledged the need for a "serious fresh start".

"In recent days, many good things have happened, but also things that have not gone well... we have to do better," said Jetten.

"And that requires in-depth talks, which we began today. This conversation is not yet complete. For that reason, I will spend the next few days continuing these talks with the three coalition parties, in a calm and measured manner," said Jetten.

It is the latest crisis in a splintered political landscape in the Netherlands that has seen four general elections in a decade and eroded public trust in the nation's lawmakers.

Jetten, the Netherlands' youngest premier, took office pledging to seek a new era of consensus among parties in the Dutch parliament, but has so far struggled to rein in political infighting among parties in the legislature and even in his own coalition.

The latest spat has raised the prospect of snap elections just nine months after Jetten's government took office.

Polls show that the left-wing PRO party and their energetic young leader Jesse Klaver would win a snap election, with far-right firebrand Geert Wilders in second place.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Estonia was preparing to potentially close its border with Russia to "reduce the risks to our people and national security."

Estonian drone manufacturer Threod Systems was the target of a Russian intelligence-ordered sabotage attack on Saturday, Prime Minister Kristen Michal said.

The attempted attack, which took place in the early hours of Saturday morning, aimed to cause an explosion and set fire to Threod's premises, according to Estonia's Internal Security Service.

In a post on social media on Sunday, Michal said "extensive damage" had been averted thanks to "heightened security measures and a swift reaction by law enforcement."

The alleged attackers have been detained, he added. Local media outlets are reporting that eight people were taken into custody in relation to the incident.

"This is part of Russia’s broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia," Michal wrote.

Founded in 2012, Threod develops and manufactures unmanned aircraft and surveillance systems such as its Eos drones and eOpic electro-optical units. The company is based in Viimsi Parish, near the Estonian capital, Tallinn.

The Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, or GRU, is Russia's military intelligence agency, and it is suspected of being behind numerous hybrid attacks on European territory in recent years.

It is believed that the agency, along with other intelligence bodies in Russia, often attempts to recruit local assets to carry out sabotage missions.

Michal said Estonia was now preparing to potentially close its border with Russia to "reduce the risks to our people and national security."

It comes after Milrem Robotics, another Estonian defence firm, was hit by an arson attack in August. Estonian officials have said that attack was ordered by Russian special services.

Sitting on NATO's eastern flank, Estonia and its Baltic neighbours have been particularly exposed to security consequences believed to stem from Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and there have been rapidly increasing reports of cyberattacks, drone incursions and sabotage attempts targeting the region.

Online shopping and digital services are growing across Southeast Asia, but businesses still face different rules in each country. ASEAN’s new agreement aims to make it easier to sell, receive payments and share data across the region.

Southeast Asian nations signed an agreement on Saturday aimed at making it easier for businesses to trade online, make payments and transfer data across borders.

The Digital Economy Framework Agreement was signed by ministers in Manila. It is the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ (ASEAN) first stand-alone, legally binding agreement on the digital economy.

It is due to take effect in May 2027, 180 days after signing, and replace the bloc’s 2019 agreement on electronic commerce, according to Singapore’s trade ministry.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. formally handed the signed agreement to ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn at the opening of the bloc’s summit on Sunday.

The pact promotes wider acceptance of electronic invoices, shipping documents and signatures to reduce paperwork. It also aims to make payment systems in different countries work together, helping businesses pay suppliers and receive money from customers abroad.

It sets rules for transferring commercial and financial data across borders, limiting requirements for companies to store that information locally, Singapore’s trade ministry said.

Singapore’s Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said exceptions would remain to address concerns over privacy, business confidentiality and national security. Countries would also be able to move at different speeds as they develop their digital systems, he told reporters after the signing.

Putting the agreement into practice

The Asian Development Bank announced on Saturday an initiative aimed at raising up to $5 billion (€4.5bn) in public and private funding by 2030 to support the agreement.

The money would help develop digital infrastructure, payment systems that work across borders and tools to verify identities online, alongside measures to improve cybersecurity.

Gan said differences in countries’ digital readiness had made negotiations difficult. Governments were now identifying projects involving payments, digital identities and electronic trade documents that could be ready when the agreement takes effect.

The deal comes as online business expands across the region. Google, Temasek and Bain & Company forecast that transactions across Southeast Asia’s main digital sectors will reach $368 billion (€333bn) this year and exceed $1 trillion(€905bn) by 2035. Their study covers 10 countries and includes online shopping, travel and food delivery.

“The key measure of success will be what businesses experience on the ground,” said Singapore Business Federation chief executive Kok Ping Soon in a statement released by the trade ministry.
